query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A workflow that uses minimal ab initio molecular‐dynamics sampling to train a machine‐learning interatomic potential, which is then coupled with efficient Monte Carlo or free‐energy integration methods, can faithfully capture the vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration entropy contributions in both the solid and fluid phases at high temperature. This approach is predicted to produce accurate fusion free-energy differences and derived thermodynamic observables at significantly lower computational cost than full ab initio MD or TOR-TILD, even for multicomponent high‐entropy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental or binary systems initially studied by ab initio methods and extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys exhibiting single-phase solid and liquid states near fusion conditions.
generation.intervention: Perform short ab initio MD simulations to generate a limited but representative configurational ensemble; use these data to train a machine-learning potential that retains anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling; then perform high-throughput Monte Carlo or accelerated free-energy integration using this potential to compute absolute free energies and entropy terms for both solid and fluid states.
generation.conditions: Applicable in the temperature range spanning from near melting to high-temperature operation, and for compositions where the sampling of local vibrational fluctuations (and moderate anharmonic effects) is representative – typically elemental, binary, and moderately complex multicomponent alloys (e.g. quaternary to quinary systems).
generation.structural_mediator: The machine-learning potential acts as the mediator by accurately reproducing chemical bonding and local vibrational correlations that determine the free-energy landscapes in both phases.
generation.mechanism: By training on a small set of high-fidelity MD data, the ML potential encapsulates the key interactions (including anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling) that govern the vibrational entropy; its use in rapid Monte Carlo or similar free-energy integration schemes then circumvents the need for long, computationally expensive explicit MD trajectories while preserving the fidelity of both phase free energies.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method should deliver fusion-related free energy differences and associated properties (e.g., latent heat, high-temperature specific heat) with errors within an acceptable threshold (e.g. within ~5% of full ab initio MD results) while reducing overall computational time by an order of magnitude or more compared to TOR-TILD and explicit MD workflows.
generation.baseline: Existing explicit ab initio MD free-energy integration methods and TOR-TILD simulations, which are accurate but computationally expensive, especially for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to work reliably for systems that do not exhibit extreme anharmonic or non-Gaussian displacement distributions (e.g. within moderate/high-temperature regimes near fusion) and for materials where the ML training set can adequately sample the relevant configurational space. Extrapolation to systems with very strong anharmonicity or largely fluctuating bonding environments might fall outside its current predictive capability.
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy of the ML potential in capturing subtle electron–vibration interactions and higher-order anharmonic contributions remains uncertain in regimes with extreme atomic displacements or very complex multicomponent compositions. The transferability of the trained potential across closely related materials and the quantification of any residual errors compared to full AIMD are also open questions.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative alloy system (e.g. a known binary metal and a moderate multicomponent high-entropy alloy) close to its fusion temperature. First, run short ab initio MD simulations to generate a training dataset and develop an ML potential. Then, perform free-energy integration using Monte Carlo sampling with the ML potential to compute the absolute free energies, latent heats, and vibrational entropy contributions for both the solid and liquid phases. In parallel, conduct full-length explicit ab initio MD simulations (or use a validated TOR-TILD approach) to obtain benchmark free-energy values.
measurements: Absolute free energies of the solid and liquid phases
Temperature-dependent specific heats or vibrational entropy estimates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the free energies, latent heat, or other derived thermodynamic quantities predicted by the ML–augmented workflow deviate by more than the predetermined acceptable error threshold (e.g. >5%) from the benchmark ab initio MD or TOR-TILD results across both phases, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Figure 1b, c shows a comparison of the DFT- and MTP-predicted energies and forces for both training and test sets. AbstractThe vibrational entropy of a solid at finite temperature is investigated from the perspective of information theory. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations generate ensembles of atomic configurations at finite temperature from which we obtain the N-body distribution of atomic displacements, ρN. We calculate the information-theoretic entropy from the expectation value of lnρN. At a first level of approximation, treating individual atomic displacements independently, our method may be applied using Debye–Waller B-factors, allowing diffraction experiments to obtain an upper bound on the thermodynamic entropy. At the next level of approximation we correct the overestimation through inclusion of displacement covariances. We apply this approach to elemental body-centered cubic sodium and face-centered cubic aluminum, showing good agreement with experimental values above the Debye temperatures of the metals. Below the Debye temperatures, we extract an effective vibrational density of states from eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, and then evaluate the entropy quantum mechanically, again yielding good agreement with experiment down to low temperatures.
